title: How a Duck Keeps Its Feathers

before.title: A Duck Stays Dry
before.text: A duck has many feathers. It uses its bill to put oil on them. The outer feathers help keep water away from the skin. Air under the feathers also helps the duck stay warm. The duck still needs clean water and time to care for its body.

after.title: How a Duck Keeps Its Feathers
after.text:
A duck spends time caring for its feathers. It uses its bill to put the feathers back in place. Their small parts fit closely together and help keep water away from its skin.

As it cleans its feathers, the duck also spreads oil from a small gland near its tail. The oil helps the feathers stay in good condition. Air held by the feathers helps keep the duck warm.

A duck needs water and time to clean and arrange its feathers. Feathers do more than cover its body; their condition matters when it swims.

reason: Oil alone does not explain waterproof plumage. Explain feather structure, preening and oil in a bounded description and preserve the clean-water need.

title: Layers in a Roman Road

before.title: Roads Built in Layers
before.text: Roman road builders often prepared the ground before placing the top stones. The exact design changed from place to place. Some roads had several layers, side ditches, and a raised center that helped water move away. These roads linked towns, forts, farms, and ports across the empire.

after.title: Layers in a Roman Road
after.text:
Roman builders made roads in different ways. The materials depended on the land and on what was nearby.

On some roads, workers raised the middle of the road. They laid stones or gravel in layers to make a firm path. Ditches at the sides helped carry water away.

These roads linked towns and other places. Parts remain today, but one surviving road cannot show how every Roman road was built.

reason: The road structure varied and stone top surfaces were not universal. Describe a possible layered gravel road with drainage rather than a single standard construction.

title: Dorothy Follows the Yellow Road

before.title: Dorothy Follows the Yellow Road
before.text: A great wind carries Dorothy and her house to Oz. She wants to return home. On a yellow road, she meets a scarecrow, a tin man, and a lion. Each wants something too. They face danger together. In the end, Dorothy learns that her silver shoes can carry her home.

after.title: Dorothy Follows the Yellow Road
after.text: A great wind carries Dorothy and her house to Oz. She wants to return home. On a yellow road, she meets a scarecrow, a tin man, and a lion. Each wants something too. They face danger together. In the end, Dorothy learns that her silver shoes can carry her home.

title: A Bat Finds an Insect

before.title: A Bat Listens for Dinner
before.text: A bat can find small insects by making high sounds. The sound hits a thing and comes back. The bat uses the sound that comes back to learn where the thing is. It can do this in the dark. A bat can also see. It does not use sound because it is blind.

after.title: A Bat Finds an Insect
after.text:
Many bats find insects by sending out high sounds. When a sound reaches an insect, part of it comes back to the bat.

The bat listens to the returning sound. It can use that sound to find an insect in the dark. This way of finding things is called echolocation.

Bats can also see. They do not use sound because they are blind. Different bats use their senses in different ways.

reason: Make clear that echolocation applies to many, not every, bats; explain reflected sound in everyday language and retain the correction that bats can see.

title: Pompeii under Ash

before.title: Pompeii under Ash
before.text: In the year 79, Mount Vesuvius sent hot rock, ash, and gas into the air. The material covered Pompeii and places near it. Many streets, homes, and things were left under the ground. Much later, people began to find parts of Pompeii again. The site helps us learn about life in a Roman town.

after.title: Pompeii under Ash
after.text:
In the year 79, Mount Vesuvius erupted near the Roman town of Pompeii. Pumice stones and ash fell on the town. Later, very hot clouds of gas and ash reached it.

The eruption killed many people and covered streets, homes and everyday objects. Long afterward, people began to uncover parts of the town.

Today, the remains help us study how people lived there. They also show how suddenly the eruption changed their lives.

reason: Keep the date and excavation claim grounded in the Pompeii Archaeological Park account. Replace “hot rock” and the ambiguous assertion that objects were left underground.

title: Why the Moon Looks Different

before.title: Why the Moon Looks Different
before.text: The Sun always lights one half of the Moon. The Moon moves around Earth. As it moves, we see more or less of its bright side. This is why its shape seems to change through the month. Earth's shadow is not the cause of these daily changes. It covers the Moon only at special times.

after.title: Why the Moon Looks Different
after.text:
Sunlight usually lights one half of the Moon. As the Moon moves around Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half.

Sometimes we see only a thin bright curve. On other nights, we see nearly the whole bright side. The Moon has not changed its shape.

Earth’s shadow does not cause these regular changes. When the Moon passes into that shadow, it is a lunar eclipse. That is a different event.

reason: The Sun usually lights half the Moon, with the eclipse as an exception; the phases depend on viewing the lit part as the Moon orbits Earth. Bound that statement and avoid suggesting Earth’s shadow causes ordinary phases.
